lines.teach-page.1: Here's a table of thirty-two customers. Each one is a row.
lines.teach-page.2: On disk, rows aren't stored one by one. They're packed into pages.

teach-page.3.caption: Every page is the same size: 8 KB.
teach-page.3.voice: Every page is the same size. Eight kilobytes.

lines.teach-page.why-ask: Now, you might be wondering about that number.

teach-page.why.caption: Disks move data in fixed-size blocks, so databases do too. Postgres uses 8 KB pages; MySQL's InnoDB uses 16 KB.
teach-page.why.voice: Disks move data in fixed-size blocks, so databases do too. Postgres uses eight kilobyte pages. MySQL's InnoDB uses sixteen.

lines.teach-page.why-2: Big enough to read efficiently. Small enough to keep thousands of them in memory.
lines.teach-page.4: A real page holds around a hundred rows. We'll draw four, so you can actually see them.
lines.teach-page.5: Here's the catch. To read one row, the engine copies its whole page into memory.
lines.page.1: Let's make that concrete. On the left, the table on disk. On the right, memory.
lines.page.predict: You're about to fetch one customer. How much will the disk actually read?
lines.page.predict-row: That's the intuitive answer. Let's find out.
lines.page.predict-table: Not quite that bad. Let's see.
lines.page.hint: Any numbered row on the shelf will do.

page.got.caption: You wanted {asked} B. The disk handed over 8,192 B.
page.got.voice: You asked for one small row. The disk handed over the whole page. Eight kilobytes.

lines.page.amp: That ratio, bytes read over bytes wanted, is called read amplification. Keep an eye on it.
lines.neighbour.1: But here's the upside. That page is sitting in memory now, with its neighbours on it.
lines.neighbour.ask: Tap one of the other rows on that page.
lines.neighbour.hint: The glowing rows share its page.

neighbour.free.caption: Free ride: +0 B read from disk.
neighbour.free.voice: Free. Zero extra bytes from disk. The page was already here.

lines.neighbour.2: Amplification drops with every neighbour you read.
lines.neighbour.3: That's why databases work so hard to store rows that are read together, together.
lines.teach-cache.1: Disk holds every page. But every read from disk is slow.
lines.teach-cache.2: RAM is fast, but it only holds a few pages. This one holds two.
lines.teach-cache.3: If the page you need isn't in RAM, that's a miss. You wait for the disk.
lines.teach-cache.4: If it's already there, that's a hit. Almost free.
lines.teach-cache.5: But RAM fills up. To load another page, one of them has to leave.
lines.teach-cache.6: Which one? We'll get to that. First, feel the difference yourself.
lines.hit.1: Here's the disk, and a RAM with two empty slots. The stopwatch times each fetch.

hit.miss.caption: Miss: 8 ms waiting on disk. Now fetch it again.
hit.miss.voice: A miss. Eight milliseconds, just waiting on the disk. Now fetch it again.

hit.hit.caption: Hit: 0.1 ms. That's 80× faster.
hit.hit.voice: A hit. A tenth of a millisecond. Eighty times faster.

lines.hit.outro: Real numbers vary, but the gap between memory and disk is always huge.
lines.bet.1: Now you call it. For each lookup, bet: is its page already in RAM?
lines.bet.2: The clue is on the cards. Each page shows which customers it holds.
lines.bet.hint: Check whether the customer's number falls inside a page in RAM.
lines.bet.wrong-hit: Nope. That page was already in RAM.
lines.bet.wrong-miss: Nope. That page wasn't in RAM.

bet.sharp.caption: {score} / {total}. You're reading the buffer pool like the engine does.
bet.sharp.voice: Sharp. You're reading the buffer pool like the engine does.

bet.ok.caption: {score} / {total}. The page ranges are the clue.
bet.ok.voice: Once you spot the page ranges, it gets easy.

teach-evict.1.caption: RAM holds P1 and P5. P1 arrived first.
teach-evict.1.voice: RAM holds page one and page five. Page one arrived first.

teach-evict.2.caption: Then P1 is used again.
teach-evict.2.voice: Then page one gets used again.

teach-evict.ask.caption: Now another page is needed, and RAM is full. Which one should leave?
teach-evict.ask.voice: Now another page is needed, and RAM is full. Which one should leave?

lines.teach-evict.p1: That's exactly what the simplest rule does. Let's compare.
lines.teach-evict.p5: That's what the smarter rule does. Let's compare.

teach-evict.3.caption: Rule 1 · FIFO: first in, first out. It evicts P1, even though P1 is busy.
teach-evict.3.voice: Rule one. FIFO: first in, first out. It evicts page one, even though page one is busy.

teach-evict.4.caption: Rule 2 · LRU: least recently used. It evicts P5.
teach-evict.4.voice: Rule two. LRU: least recently used. It evicts page five.

teach-evict.5.caption: Busy pages should stay, so real databases use LRU-like rules.
teach-evict.5.voice: Busy pages should stay. So real databases use rules like LRU.

evict.1.caption: Customer #26 needs P7, and RAM is full.
evict.1.voice: Customer twenty-six needs page seven, and RAM is full.

lines.evict.ask: Which page would LRU evict? Tap it.
lines.evict.hint: Look at when each page was last used.

evict.right.caption: Right: P8 was used longest ago. LRU keeps busy P4.
evict.right.voice: Right. Page eight was used longest ago, so it goes. Busy page four stays.

evict.wrong.caption: That's FIFO's pick. LRU evicts P8, used longest ago.
evict.wrong.voice: Not quite. That's what FIFO would pick. LRU evicts page eight, the one used longest ago.

race.1.caption: In this workload, P1 🔥 is needed on every other lookup. It's hot.
race.1.voice: In this workload, page one is needed on every other lookup. It's hot.

lines.race.predict: FIFO against LRU, same lookups. Which one goes to disk less?
lines.race.hint: The Go button starts the race.

race.result.caption: LRU: {lru} disk reads. FIFO: {fifo}.
race.result.voice: LRU made fewer trips to disk.

lines.race.explain: FIFO keeps throwing out the hot page just for being old. LRU refreshes it on every use, so it never leaves.

teach-locality.1.caption: GET /orders shows Maya's 12 latest orders.
teach-locality.1.voice: An orders endpoint shows Maya's twelve latest orders.

lines.teach-locality.2: They were written over two years, so they're scattered across the table's pages.
lines.teach-locality.3: An index says where each order is. Following it costs one jump per page.

teach-locality.4.caption: A covering index stores the orders themselves, sorted: a few neighbouring pages.
teach-locality.4.voice: A covering index stores the orders themselves, in order. So they sit on a few neighbouring pages.

lines.head.1: Now you're the read head. Every page you touch costs a trip to disk.
lines.head.ask: Tap the glowing page, and keep following it.

head.phase.caption: 10 jumps, 80 ms. Now the covering index.
head.phase.voice: Ten jumps. Eighty milliseconds. Now try the covering index.

head.result.caption: Same 12 rows: 10 scattered pages vs 3 neighbours.
head.result.voice: Same twelve rows. Ten scattered pages, versus three neighbours.

lines.head.outro: Under a third of the time, just from storing rows that are read together, together.
lines.cache.1: One more twist. Everything so far assumed a cold cache, like right after a restart.
lines.cache.ask: Flip the switch to warm the cache.
lines.cache.hint: Tap the switch between Cold and Warm.

cache.warm.caption: Warm RAM hides the jumps. Staging lies.
cache.warm.voice: With a warm cache, both paths are fast. The jumps are hidden.

lines.cache.2: That's why this bug hides in staging, then shows up after a restart, a failover, or once the data outgrows memory.
lines.cache.ram: More RAM helps, until the data outgrows it, or the server restarts. Fixing the access pattern keeps working either way.

quiz.q1.caption: You ask for customer #11, a 70-byte row. What does the engine read from storage?
quiz.q1.voice: You ask for customer eleven, a seventy-byte row. What does the engine read from storage?
quiz.q1.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q1-why: Storage moves whole pages. The row you wanted arrives with every neighbour on its page.

quiz.q2.caption: #12 sits on the same page as #11, which you fetched a moment ago. Fetching #12 next is most likely…
quiz.q2.voice: Customer twelve sits on the same page as eleven, which you just fetched. Fetching twelve next is most likely what?
quiz.q2.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q2-why: The page came into memory with eleven, so twelve is a buffer hit. Neighbours ride along for free.

quiz.q3.caption: A buffer pool has 2 slots. One page is needed by every other query. Which eviction rule keeps it in memory?
quiz.q3.voice: A buffer pool has two slots. One page is needed by every other query. Which eviction rule keeps it in memory?
quiz.q3.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q3-why: LRU refreshes a page every time it's used, so a hot page never becomes the oldest. FIFO evicts by arrival, even if the page was just used.

quiz.q4.caption: GET /orders returns 12 rows but reads 10 scattered pages on a cold cache. Best first fix?
quiz.q4.voice: An orders endpoint returns twelve rows, but reads ten scattered pages on a cold cache. What's the best first fix?
quiz.q4.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q4-why: The rows are few, but scattered. An index in the query's order, holding the columns it shows, turns ten random pages into a few neighbouring ones.

quiz.retry.caption: {right} / 4. Worth another pass.
quiz.retry.voice: Not quite there. Replay a chapter or two, then try again.

lines.finish.1: That's the lesson. Databases read pages, not rows. Hits are cheap, misses are slow, and rows stored together are read together.
lines.finish.2: Next up: how tables and indexes are actually laid out on disk.
